claim: C-tactile afferents form a distinct channel that encodes pleasant tactile stimulation.
source: C-tactile afferents form a distinct channel that encodes pleasant tactile stimulation.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific understanding about C-tactile afferents.

claim: Prevailing views indicate C-tactile afferents project, as with other unmyelinated afferents, in lamina I-spinothalamic pathways.
source: Prevailing views indicate they project, as with other unmyelinated afferents, in lamina I-spinothalamic pathways.
evidence: This statement references the existing scientific consensus about C-tactile projection pathways.

claim: Spinothalamic ablation in humans profoundly impairs pain, temperature and itch.
source: However, we found that spinothalamic ablation in humans, whilst profoundly impairing pain, temperature and itch, had no effect on pleasant touch perception.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Spinothalamic ablation in humans had no effect on pleasant touch perception.
source: However, we found that spinothalamic ablation in humans, whilst profoundly impairing pain, temperature and itch, had no effect on pleasant touch perception.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Only discriminative touch deficits were seen following spinothalamic ablation.
source: Only discriminative touch deficits were seen.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The findings preclude privileged C-tactile-lamina I-spinothalamic projections.
source: These findings preclude privileged C-tactile-lamina I-spinothalamic projections and imply integrated hedonic and discriminative spinal processing from the body.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings that pleasant touch was preserved after spinothalamic ablation.

claim: The findings imply integrated hedonic and discriminative spinal processing from the body.
source: These findings preclude privileged C-tactile-lamina I-spinothalamic projections and imply integrated hedonic and discriminative spinal processing from the body.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Touch has an affective dimension of fundamental importance to physical, emotional and social well-being, both developmentally and throughout life.
source: In addition to a well-defined discriminative role, touch has an affective dimension of fundamental importance to physical, emotional and social well-being, both developmentally and throughout life (McGlone et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to McGlone et al., 2014.

claim: C-tactile afferents are a subclass of unmyelinated low threshold mechanosensitive C-fibers innervating human hairy skin.
source: C-tactile afferents, a subclass of unmyelinated low threshold mechanosensitive C-fibers innervating human hairy skin, are strongly implicated as the neurobiological substrate subserving the affective and rewarding properties of touch (McGlone et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about C-tactile afferents supported by citation.

claim: C-tactile afferents are strongly implicated as the neurobiological substrate subserving the affective and rewarding properties of touch.
source: C-tactile afferents, a subclass of unmyelinated low threshold mechanosensitive C-fibers innervating human hairy skin, are strongly implicated as the neurobiological substrate subserving the affective and rewarding properties of touch (McGlone et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to McGlone et al., 2014.

claim: C-tactile afferents have slow conduction velocities (~1 m s−1).
source: C-tactile afferents have slow conduction velocities (~1 m s−1) which, along with other neurophysiological properties such as fatigue to repeated stimulation, makes them poorly suited for tactile discrimination (Vallbo et al., 1999; Olausson et al., 2010; McGlone et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about C-tactile afferents supported by citations.

claim: C-tactile afferents show fatigue to repeated stimulation.
source: C-tactile afferents have slow conduction velocities (~1 m s−1) which, along with other neurophysiological properties such as fatigue to repeated stimulation, makes them poorly suited for tactile discrimination (Vallbo et al., 1999; Olausson et al., 2010; McGlone et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about C-tactile afferents supported by citations.

claim: C-tactile afferents are poorly suited for tactile discrimination.
source: C-tactile afferents have slow conduction velocities (~1 m s−1) which, along with other neurophysiological properties such as fatigue to repeated stimulation, makes them poorly suited for tactile discrimination (Vallbo et al., 1999; Olausson et al., 2010; McGlone et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the neurophysiological properties of C-tactile afferents, supported by citations.

claim: C-tactile afferents preferentially respond to tactile velocities and forces typical of a gentle caress.
source: Instead, microneurography and psychophysical investigations indicate that C-tactile afferents preferentially respond to tactile velocities and forces typical of a gentle caress (Löken et al., 2009; Ackerley et al., 2014a) with peak firing rates that positively correlate with perceived touch pleasantness (Löken et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to microneurography and psychophysical studies.

claim: C-tactile afferents have peak firing rates that positively correlate with perceived touch pleasantness.
source: Instead, microneurography and psychophysical investigations indicate that C-tactile afferents preferentially respond to tactile velocities and forces typical of a gentle caress (Löken et al., 2009; Ackerley et al., 2014a) with peak firing rates that positively correlate with perceived touch pleasantness (Löken et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Löken et al., 2009.

claim: Selective C-tactile stimulation activates contralateral posterior insula cortex.
source: In keeping with a role in signalling the affective aspects of touch, selective C-tactile stimulation activates contralateral posterior insula cortex (Olausson et al., 2002; Olausson et al., 2008), a region considered a gateway for sensory systems to emotional cortical areas (Craig, 2008), but not somatosensory areas S1 and S2 (Olausson et al., 2002; Olausson et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Olausson et al., 2002 and 2008.

claim: Posterior insula cortex is considered a gateway for sensory systems to emotional cortical areas.
source: In keeping with a role in signalling the affective aspects of touch, selective C-tactile stimulation activates contralateral posterior insula cortex (Olausson et al., 2002; Olausson et al., 2008), a region considered a gateway for sensory systems to emotional cortical areas (Craig, 2008), but not somatosensory areas S1 and S2 (Olausson et al., 2002; Olausson et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Craig, 2008.

claim: Selective C-tactile stimulation does not activate somatosensory areas S1 and S2.
source: In keeping with a role in signalling the affective aspects of touch, selective C-tactile stimulation activates contralateral posterior insula cortex (Olausson et al., 2002; Olausson et al., 2008), a region considered a gateway for sensory systems to emotional cortical areas (Craig, 2008), but not somatosensory areas S1 and S2 (Olausson et al., 2002; Olausson et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Olausson et al., 2002 and 2008.

claim: Patients with ischemic stroke affecting the posterior contralateral opercular-insular cortex demonstrate impairments in the perception of C-tactile optimal touch.
source: In addition, patients with ischemic stroke affecting the posterior contralateral opercular-insular cortex demonstrate impairments in the perception of C-tactile optimal touch (Kirsch et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Kirsch et al., 2019.

claim: Posterior insula activation is not modulated by C-tactile optimal stimulation in individuals with congenital C-fiber denervation.
source: Likewise, posterior insula activation is not modulated by C-tactile optimal stimulation in individuals with congenital C-fiber denervation (Morrison et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Morrison et al., 2011.

claim: C-tactile-mediated affective touch pathways are proposed to diverge from the Aβ low threshold mechanoreceptor afferent dorsal column/medial-lemniscal discriminative touch stream.
source: C-tactile-mediated affective touch pathways are, therefore, proposed to diverge from the Aβ low threshold mechanoreceptor afferent dorsal column/medial-lemniscal discriminative touch stream and form a distinct coding channel projecting primarily to emotional rather than classical somatosensory cortical regions (Craig, 2002; Morrison et al., 2010; McGlone et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Craig, 2002; Morrison et al., 2010; McGlone et al., 2014.

claim: C-tactile-mediated affective touch pathways form a distinct coding channel projecting primarily to emotional rather than classical somatosensory cortical regions.
source: C-tactile-mediated affective touch pathways are, therefore, proposed to diverge from the Aβ low threshold mechanoreceptor afferent dorsal column/medial-lemniscal discriminative touch stream and form a distinct coding channel projecting primarily to emotional rather than classical somatosensory cortical regions (Craig, 2002; Morrison et al., 2010; McGlone et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Craig, 2002; Morrison et al., 2010; McGlone et al., 2014.

claim: The major somatosensory input into primate dorsal posterior insular cortex arises from the posterior ventral medial nucleus of thalamus.
source: The major somatosensory input into primate dorsal posterior insular cortex arise from the posterior ventral medial nucleus of thalamus (Craig et al., 1994; Craig and Zhang, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Craig et al., 1994 and Craig and Zhang, 2006.

claim: Spinal inputs to the posterior ventral medial nucleus of thalamus derive, almost exclusively, from projection cells in dorsal horn lamina I via the spinothalamic tract.
source: Spinal inputs to this thalamic relay derive, almost exclusively, from projection cells in dorsal horn lamina I via the spinothalamic tract (Craig and Zhang, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Craig and Zhang, 2006.

claim: The central terminals of C-low threshold mechanosensitive receptor (C-LTMR) afferents arborise in laminae II/IIIi of the spinal cord dorsal horn.
source: The central terminals of C-low threshold mechanosensitive receptor (C-LTMR) afferents, the animal equivalent of C-tactile afferents, arborise in laminae II/IIIi of the spinal cord dorsal horn (Light and Perl, 1979; Sugiura, 1996; Li et al., 2011; Abraira and Ginty, 2013; Larsson and Broman, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: C-LTMR afferents are the animal equivalent of C-tactile afferents.
source: The central terminals of C-low threshold mechanosensitive receptor (C-LTMR) afferents, the animal equivalent of C-tactile afferents, arborise in laminae II/IIIi of the spinal cord dorsal horn (Light and Perl, 1979; Sugiura, 1996; Li et al., 2011; Abraira and Ginty, 2013; Larsson and Broman, 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the relationship between C-LTMR and C-tactile afferents.

claim: Lamina II cells activated by C-LTMR afferents arborise in lamina I.
source: Lamina II cells activated by C-LTMR afferents arborise in lamina I (Lu and Perl, 2005; Maxwell et al., 2007; Lu et al., 2013) where they can contact projection neurons (Lu et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Lu and Perl, 2005; Maxwell et al., 2007; Lu et al., 2013.

claim: Lamina II cells activated by C-LTMR afferents can contact projection neurons in lamina I.
source: Lamina II cells activated by C-LTMR afferents arborise in lamina I (Lu and Perl, 2005; Maxwell et al., 2007; Lu et al., 2013) where they can contact projection neurons (Lu et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Lu et al., 2013.

claim: The 'dual pathway' model of discriminative and emotional touch predicts that signals arising from C-tactile activation diverge from dorsal column-bound Aβ inputs to ascend alongside other small-diameter primary afferent modalities in the lamina I spinothalamic pathway.
source: Thus, the 'dual pathway' model of discriminative and emotional touch predicts that signals arising from C-tactile activation diverge from dorsal column-bound Aβ inputs to ascend alongside other small-diameter primary afferent modalities in the lamina I spinothalamic pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical and functional evidence presented about C-tactile pathways.

claim: The spinothalamic tract lies within the anterolateral funiculus of the spinal cord.
source: Accordingly, disruption of the spinothalamic tract, which lies within the anterolateral funiculus of the spinal cord, would, in addition to causing contralateral deficits in classical spinothalamic modalities of pain, temperature and itch, be predicted to induce alterations in affective but not discriminative touch domains.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Disruption of the spinothalamic tract would be predicted to cause contralateral deficits in classical spinothalamic modalities of pain, temperature and itch.
source: Accordingly, disruption of the spinothalamic tract, which lies within the anterolateral funiculus of the spinal cord, would, in addition to causing contralateral deficits in classical spinothalamic modalities of pain, temperature and itch, be predicted to induce alterations in affective but not discriminative touch domains.
evidence: This is a prediction based on established knowledge about spinothalamic tract function.

claim: Disruption of the spinothalamic tract would be predicted to induce alterations in affective but not discriminative touch domains.
source: Accordingly, disruption of the spinothalamic tract, which lies within the anterolateral funiculus of the spinal cord, would, in addition to causing contralateral deficits in classical spinothalamic modalities of pain, temperature and itch, be predicted to induce alterations in affective but not discriminative touch domains.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the dual pathway model of touch.

claim: Assessment of noxious and innocuous temperature, itch and noxious mechanical sensation as well as discriminative and affective aspects of touch were performed on the pain-affected and unaffected sides in 19 patients undergoing anterolateral cordotomy.
source: Assessment of noxious and innocuous temperature, itch and noxious mechanical sensation as well as discriminative and affective aspects of touch were performed on the pain-affected and unaffected sides in 19 patients undergoing anterolateral cordotomy.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and methods used in the study.

claim: All sensory testing was performed on hairy skin of the dorsal forearm distant to the sites of clinical pain.
source: All sensory testing was performed on hairy skin of the dorsal forearm distant to the sites of clinical pain.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods.

claim: No patient had pre-existing neurological deficits in the area of testing.
source: No patient had pre-existing neurological deficits in the area of testing.
evidence: This describes the patient characteristics in the study.

claim: The cordotomy was performed percutaneously at cervical level C1/C2 on the side contralateral to clinical pain.
source: The cordotomy was performed percutaneously at cervical level C1/C2 on the side contralateral to clinical pain.
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure used in the study.

claim: Lesioning was performed using a radiofrequency current to produce heat-induced lesions targeting the spinothalamic tract.
source: Lesioning was performed using a radiofrequency current to produce heat-induced lesions targeting the spinothalamic tract (for clinical and procedural-related information see Materials and methods and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure used in the study.

claim: Anterolateral cordotomy induced clear-cut contralateral deficits in canonical spinothalamic modalities.
source: As expected, anterolateral cordotomy induced clear-cut contralateral deficits in canonical spinothalamic modalities: there was striking amelioration of clinical pain (Supplementary file 1); perceptual thresholds for innocuous temperature and thermal pain were markedly elevated (Related-Samples Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test all p<0.0005) (Figure 1c and d and Supplementary file 2a) and in the majority of patients thermal sensibility was abolished; Cowhage-induced itch was abolished (Supplementary file 2a).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: There was striking amelioration of clinical pain following anterolateral cordotomy.
source: As expected, anterolateral cordotomy induced clear-cut contralateral deficits in canonical spinothalamic modalities: there was striking amelioration of clinical pain (Supplementary file 1); perceptual thresholds for innocuous temperature and thermal pain were markedly elevated (Related-Samples Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test all p<0.0005) (Figure 1c and d and Supplementary file 2a) and in the majority of patients thermal sensibility was abolished; Cowhage-induced itch was abolished (Supplementary file 2a).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Perceptual thresholds for innocuous temperature and thermal pain were markedly elevated following anterolateral cordotomy (p<0.0005).
source: As expected, anterolateral cordotomy induced clear-cut contralateral deficits in canonical spinothalamic modalities: there was striking amelioration of clinical pain (Supplementary file 1); perceptual thresholds for innocuous temperature and thermal pain were markedly elevated (Related-Samples Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test all p<0.0005) (Figure 1c and d and Supplementary file 2a) and in the majority of patients thermal sensibility was abolished; Cowhage-induced itch was abolished (Supplementary file 2a).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data and statistical analysis, shown in Figure 1c and d.

claim: In the majority of patients thermal sensibility was abolished following anterolateral cordotomy.
source: As expected, anterolateral cordotomy induced clear-cut contralateral deficits in canonical spinothalamic modalities: there was striking amelioration of clinical pain (Supplementary file 1); perceptual thresholds for innocuous temperature and thermal pain were markedly elevated (Related-Samples Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test all p<0.0005) (Figure 1c and d and Supplementary file 2a) and in the majority of patients thermal sensibility was abolished; Cowhage-induced itch was abolished (Supplementary file 2a).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Cowhage-induced itch was abolished following anterolateral cordotomy.
source: As expected, anterolateral cordotomy induced clear-cut contralateral deficits in canonical spinothalamic modalities: there was striking amelioration of clinical pain (Supplementary file 1); perceptual thresholds for innocuous temperature and thermal pain were markedly elevated (Related-Samples Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test all p<0.0005) (Figure 1c and d and Supplementary file 2a) and in the majority of patients thermal sensibility was abolished; Cowhage-induced itch was abolished (Supplementary file 2a).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Tactile acuity and graphesthesia were unchanged following anterolateral cordotomy.
source: In contrast tactile acuity and graphesthesia were unchanged (Supplementary file 2a).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The findings confirm marked cordotomy-induced disruption of lamina I spinothalamic pathways.
source: These findings, therefore, confirm marked cordotomy-induced disruption of lamina I spinothalamic pathways.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed deficits in spinothalamic modalities.

claim: C-tactile afferents respond optimally to gentle skin stroking.
source: C-tactile afferents respond optimally to gentle skin stroking and display peak firing rates to stroking stimuli delivered with velocities of ~3 cm s−1 (Löken et al., 2009; Ackerley et al., 2014a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Löken et al., 2009 and Ackerley et al., 2014a.

claim: C-tactile afferents display peak firing rates to stroking stimuli delivered with velocities of ~3 cm s−1.
source: C-tactile afferents respond optimally to gentle skin stroking and display peak firing rates to stroking stimuli delivered with velocities of ~3 cm s−1 (Löken et al., 2009; Ackerley et al., 2014a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Löken et al., 2009 and Ackerley et al., 2014a.

claim: The inverted U-shaped relationship of the neural response to brushing velocity is matched by subjective ratings of touch pleasantness.
source: The resulting inverted U-shaped relationship of the neural response to brushing velocity is, critically, matched by subjective ratings of touch pleasantness (Löken et al., 2009; Ackerley et al., 2014a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Löken et al., 2009 and Ackerley et al., 2014a.

claim: Pre-cordotomy visual analogue scale (VAS) ratings for touch pleasantness to gentle brushing stimuli were greater to stroking at 3 cm s−1 than at 0.3 and 30 cm s−1.
source: Correspondingly, pre-cordotomy visual analogue scale (VAS) ratings for touch pleasantness to gentle brushing stimuli were greater to stroking at 3 cm s−1 than at 0.3 and 30 cm s−1 (Figure 2a - d).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Cordotomy did not affect ratings for touch pleasantness.
source: However, cordotomy did not affect ratings for touch pleasantness (Figure 2a- d and Supplementary file 2b).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: A negative quadratic regressor provided a better fit than a linear regressor for brush velocity and VAS scores for all four conditions (F test, p=0.001–0.003).
source: Regression analysis of brush velocity and VAS scores for all four conditions showed that a negative quadratic regressor provided a better fit than a linear regressor (F test, p=0.001–0.003).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis result from the study data.

claim: The negative quadratic term, β2, and extracted Y-intercept values for individual patients were not significantly altered by cordotomy.
source: The negative quadratic term, β2, and extracted Y-intercept values for individual patients, which provide measures of the degree of the inverted U-shape and overall perceived touch pleasantness across all velocities respectively, were not significantly altered by cordotomy (Figure 2d-f and Supplementary Table 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: For individual patients a negative quadratic regressor provided a better fit than a linear regressor (F test, p=0.05 or less) for 14/19 (pre-cordotomy pain affected, pre-cordotomy control) and 13/19 (post-cordotomy pain affected and post-cordotomy control) patients.
source: For individual patients a negative quadratic regressor provided a better fit than a linear regressor (F test, p=0.05 or less) for 14/19 (pre-cordotomy pain affected, pre-cordotomy control) and 13/19 (post-cordotomy pain affected and post-cordotomy control) patients.
evidence: This is a statistical analysis result from the study data.

claim: Ratings of touch intensity show a close correlation with A-β low threshold mechanoreceptor afferent firing rates.
source: Ratings of touch intensity, which show a close correlation with A-β low threshold mechanoreceptor afferent firing rates, increased with increasing brushing velocity as expected (Figure 3a-c) (Löken et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Löken et al., 2009.

claim: Ratings of touch intensity increased with increasing brushing velocity.
source: Ratings of touch intensity, which show a close correlation with A-β low threshold mechanoreceptor afferent firing rates, increased with increasing brushing velocity as expected (Figure 3a-c) (Löken et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: VAS touch intensity across all velocities was significantly lower following cordotomy in the pain-affected side.
source: This pattern was present in all conditions, however, VAS touch intensity across all velocities was significantly lower following cordotomy in the pain-affected side (Figure 3a-b and Supplementary file 2b).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Ratings for both touch pleasantness and intensity on the control side (i.e. ipsilateral to the cordotomy lesion) were unaffected by anterolateral cordotomy.
source: Ratings for both touch pleasantness and intensity on the control side (i.e. ipsilateral to the cordotomy lesion) were unaffected by anterolateral cordotomy.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Touch intensity is a generally accepted discriminative function.
source: Therefore, counter to our prediction that spinothalamic tract lesioning would reduce the pleasant properties of touch, we found instead that touch intensity – a generally accepted discriminative function - was reduced.
evidence: This is established knowledge about touch intensity.

claim: Relative to hairy skin, gentle stroking of skin lacking C-tactile innervation (e.g. palmar glabrous skin) results in lower ratings for positive emotionally relevant terms (e.g. calming and comfortable).
source: Relative to hairy skin, gentle stroking of skin lacking C-tactile innervation (e.g. palmar glabrous skin) results in lower ratings for positive emotionally relevant terms (e.g. calming and comfortable) (Ackerley et al., 2014b; McGlone et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ackerley et al., 2014b and McGlone et al., 2012.

claim: Prior to cordotomy, stroking with fur resulted in high mean descriptor ratings and weighted factor scores for positive emotional terms, as well as discriminative terms relating to surface pile (e.g. fluffy, soft).
source: Prior to cordotomy, stroking with fur resulted in high mean descriptor ratings and weighted factor scores for positive emotional terms, as well as discriminative terms relating to surface pile (e.g. fluffy, soft) (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Ratings and weighted factor scores for positive emotional terms and discriminative terms relating to surface pile were unaffected by cordotomy for stroking with fur.
source: However, these were all unaffected by cordotomy, further supporting the finding that following spinothalamic tract disruption the emotional descriptive profile for soft stroking of hairy skin does not shift towards that seen with stimulation of skin lacking C-tactile innervation (Figure 4a-g) (McGlone et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Following spinothalamic tract disruption the emotional descriptive profile for soft stroking of hairy skin does not shift towards that seen with stimulation of skin lacking C-tactile innervation.
source: However, these were all unaffected by cordotomy, further supporting the finding that following spinothalamic tract disruption the emotional descriptive profile for soft stroking of hairy skin does not shift towards that seen with stimulation of skin lacking C-tactile innervation (Figure 4a-g) (McGlone et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and comparison with cited literature.

claim: For stimulation with sandpaper, lesioning significantly attenuated roughness perception.
source: In contrast, for stimulation with sandpaper, which is an unpleasant stimulus, lesioning significantly attenuated roughness perception (Figure 4a-b) and, concomitantly, shifted the affective valance of tactile sensation from negative to positive (Figure 4a,f and g).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: For stimulation with sandpaper, lesioning shifted the affective valance of tactile sensation from negative to positive.
source: In contrast, for stimulation with sandpaper, which is an unpleasant stimulus, lesioning significantly attenuated roughness perception (Figure 4a-b) and, concomitantly, shifted the affective valance of tactile sensation from negative to positive (Figure 4a,f and g).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Ratings for both sensory and emotional descriptor terms were unaffected on the control side.
source: Ratings for both sensory and emotional descriptor terms were unaffected on the control side (Figure 4a-g).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The development of a velocity-tuned preference to slow touch is dependent on the activity of small diameter afferents, presumably C-tactile fibers.
source: The development of a velocity-tuned preference to slow touch is dependent on the activity of small diameter afferents, presumably C-tactile fibers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the evidence presented in the manuscript.

claim: Patients who have congenital C-fiber denervation, but normal A-β fiber function, lack the inverted U-shaped relationship between stroking velocity and pleasantness.
source: Patients who have congenital C-fiber denervation, but normal A-β fiber function, lack the inverted U-shaped relationship between stroking velocity and pleasantness (Morrison et al., 2011; Macefield et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Morrison et al., 2011 and Macefield et al., 2014.

claim: Patients with congenital C-fiber denervation show rating patterns that indicate a reliance on A-β low threshold mechanosensitive receptor afferent inputs.
source: Instead, their rating patterns indicate a reliance on A-β low threshold mechanosensitive receptor afferent inputs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited studies of patients with congenital C-fiber denervation.

claim: If there were a dedicated lamina I spinothalamic coding channel responsible for the perception of affective aspects of touch one would expect post-cordotomy affective touch metrics to shift towards those seen in patients with congenital C-fiber denervation.
source: If there were a dedicated lamina I spinothalamic coding channel responsible for the perception of affective aspects of touch one would expect post-cordotomy affective touch metrics to shift towards those seen in patients with congenital C-fiber denervation.
evidence: This is a logical prediction based on the dual pathway model.

claim: Unlike the unambiguous absence of the perceptions of temperature, itch and pain following anterolateral cordotomy, judgments about touch pleasantness, including that predicated on distinctive velocity tuned C-tactile responses, were unaltered.
source: However, here we have shown that, unlike the unambiguous absence of the perceptions of temperature, itch and pain following anterolateral cordotomy, judgments about touch pleasantness, including that predicated on distinctive velocity tuned C-tactile responses, were unaltered.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Slow, stroking stimuli targeting C-LTMR afferents elicit velocity tuned responses in lamina I projection neurons in rats.
source: Slow, stroking stimuli targeting C-LTMR afferents do elicit velocity tuned responses in lamina I projection neurons in rats (Andrew, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Andrew, 2010.

claim: Lamina I projection neurons that respond to C-LTMR afferents are wide dynamic range and also respond to noxious stimuli.
source: These projection neurons are, however, wide dynamic range and also respond to noxious stimuli (Andrew, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Andrew, 2010.

claim: C-LTMR terminals in dorsal horn lamina IIi that connect to lamina I projection neurons do so via an interneuronal relay subject to complex regulation.
source: Furthermore, C-LTMR terminals in dorsal horn lamina IIi that connect to lamina I projection neurons (Lu and Perl, 2003; Maxwell et al., 2007; Lu et al., 2013) do so via an interneuronal relay subject to complex regulation (Larsson and Broman, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Lu and Perl, 2003; Maxwell et al., 2007; Lu et al., 2013; Larsson and Broman, 2019.

claim: Rodent C-LTMR afferents access the dorsal column pathway.
source: Other recent evidence suggests that rodent C-LTMR afferents access the dorsal column pathway (Abraira et al., 2017) via the interneuronal rich dorsal horn zone spanning lamina IIiv through lamina V that receives synapses from myelinated and unmyelinated low threshold mechanosensitive receptor subtypes (Li et al., 2011; Abraira and Ginty, 2013; Abraira et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Abraira et al., 2017 and related studies.

claim: Integrated outputs from the dorsal horn zone spanning lamina IIiv through lamina V target the indirect, post-synaptic dorsal column pathway.
source: Integrated outputs from this recipient zone target the indirect, post-synaptic dorsal column pathway (Abraira et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Abraira et al., 2017.

claim: C-LTMR terminals in the dorsal horn show precise somatotopic arrangement with little overlap.
source: C-LTMR terminals in the dorsal horn paradoxically, given the poor spatial resolution of C-tactile-mediated touch (Olausson et al., 2002; McGlone et al., 2014; Olausson et al., 2007), show precise somatotopic arrangement with little overlap (Kuehn et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Kuehn et al., 2019.

claim: C-LTMR afferents shape the processing of hairy skin A-β subtypes in 'somatotopically relevant' manner.
source: This suggests that C-LTMR afferents, rather than signalling directly, shape the processing of hairy skin A-β subtypes in 'somatotopically relevant' manner (Kuehn et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited evidence about somatotopic arrangement.

claim: The cordotomy patients may have learned to associate certain tactile velocities with touch pleasantness and thus rely purely on ascending A-β low threshold mechanoreceptor afferent inputs when making judgements about the affective/emotional properties of touch.
source: Whilst the emerging realization of the complexity of processing of tactile information at the earliest central nervous system relay (Abraira et al., 2017) suggests a more complex explanation it is conceivable that the cordotomy patients may have learned to associate certain tactile velocities with touch pleasantness and thus rely purely on ascending A-β low threshold mechanoreceptor afferent inputs when making judgements about the affective/emotional properties of touch.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the findings.

claim: In individuals with a neurodevelopmentally normal somatosensory system, fibers ascending outside the anterolateral funiculus, most likely within the dorsal columns, provide sufficient information to conserve judgements about touch pleasantness.
source: In either case the current findings indicate in individuals with a neurodevelopmentally normal somatosensory system that fibers ascending outside the anterolateral funiculus, most likely within the dorsal columns, provide sufficient information to conserve judgements about touch pleasantness.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: A contralateral reduction in ratings for the intensity of stroking touch across all velocities was seen following anterolateral cordotomy although monofilament tactile detection thresholds were not affected.
source: A contralateral reduction in ratings for the intensity of stroking touch across all velocities was seen following anterolateral cordotomy although monofilament tactile detection thresholds were not affected.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: It is unlikely that the reduction in touch intensity relates to a selective loss of ascending C-tactile inputs.
source: It is unlikely that these effects relate to a selective loss of ascending C-tactile inputs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the evidence about C-tactile function.

claim: C-tactile afferents contribute to the relative preservation of monofilament tactile detection in A-β denervated individuals and under conditions of A-fiber blockade.
source: There is evidence that C-tactile afferents contribute to the relative preservation of monofilament tactile detection in A-β denervated individuals and under conditions of A-fiber blockade (Cole et al., 2006; Nagi et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Cole et al., 2006 and Nagi et al., 2015.

claim: C-tactile afferent mean firing rates do not correlate with the touch intensity ratings that increase in parallel stroking velocity.
source: However, their mean firing rates, unlike those of A-beta afferent LTMRs, do not correlate with the touch intensity ratings that increase in parallel stroking velocity (Löken et al., 2009; Ackerley et al., 2014a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Löken et al., 2009 and Ackerley et al., 2014a.

claim: The current findings support an integrative model of hedonic touch for human hairy skin.
source: The current findings support such an integrative model of hedonic touch also for human hairy skin.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: The current findings are incompatible with a segregated model of touch where emotional and discriminative elements are signaled in anatomically discrete second order pathways.
source: They are, in fact, incompatible with a segregated model of touch where emotional and discriminative elements are signaled in anatomically discrete second order pathways.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: For hairy skin, tactile information quintessentially regarded as discriminative and dependent on A-β activity also partly relays in crossed pathways ascending the anterolateral funiculus.
source: Indeed, the contralateral attenuations of texture perception and touch intensity seen post-cordotomy indicate that, for hairy skin, tactile information quintessentially regarded as discriminative and dependent on A-β activity (Saal and Bensmaia, 2014; Manfredi et al., 2014; Lieber et al., 2017), also partly relays in crossed pathways ascending the anterolateral funiculus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and cited literature.

claim: Twenty patients were recruited in accordance with the Health Research Authority National Research Ethics Service (study reference 14/NW/1247).
source: Twenty patients were recruited in accordance with the Health Research Authority National Research Ethics Service (study reference 14/NW/1247).
evidence: This describes the study design and ethical approval.

claim: The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
source: The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
evidence: This describes the ethical standards of the study.

claim: All patients were admitted to the Walton Centre, Liverpool, UK and suffered from intractable unilateral cancer-related pain below the cervical level C4 with an expected lifespan of less than 12 months.
source: All patients were admitted to the Walton Centre, Liverpool, UK and suffered from intractable unilateral cancer-related pain below the cervical level C4 with an expected lifespan of less than 12 months.
evidence: This describes the patient population in the study.

claim: It was not possible to test one patient in the post-operative state.
source: It was not possible to test one patient in the post-operative state.
evidence: This describes a limitation in the study data collection.

claim: Of the 19 patients nine were female.
source: Of the 19 patients nine were female.
evidence: This describes the demographic characteristics of the study population.

claim: All patients were medicated with regular and pro re nata opioids as well as a variety of non-opioid analgesia.
source: All patients were medicated with regular and pro re nata opioids as well as a variety of non-opioid analgesia.
evidence: This describes the medication status of the study population.

claim: The median and range for numeric rating scale of average 4 hr pain, maximum pain in the past 4 hr and current pain were 76 (20-90), 98 (79-100) and 50 (10-81) respectively.
source: The median and range for numeric rating scale of average 4 hr pain, maximum pain in the past 4 hr and current pain were 76 (20-90), 98 (79-100) and 50 (10-81) respectively.
evidence: This describes the pain characteristics of the study population.

claim: A large number (13/19) of patients had previously received chemotherapy with potential peripheral neurotoxicity although no patient described ongoing symptoms potentially attributable to this.
source: A large number (13/19) of patients had previously received chemotherapy with potential peripheral neurotoxicity although no patient described ongoing symptoms potentially attributable to this.
evidence: This describes the medical history of the study population.

claim: Pre-procedural thermal and thermal pain detection thresholds were normal in the area of sensory testing.
source: However, pre-procedural thermal and thermal pain detection thresholds were normal in the area of sensory testing and there was no pre-procedural evidence of impaired sensory discriminative or affective touch (see main article).
evidence: This describes the baseline sensory function of the study population.

claim: There was no pre-procedural evidence of impaired sensory discriminative or affective touch.
source: However, pre-procedural thermal and thermal pain detection thresholds were normal in the area of sensory testing and there was no pre-procedural evidence of impaired sensory discriminative or affective touch (see main article).
evidence: This describes the baseline sensory function of the study population.

claim: Antero-lateral cordotomy was performed at the cervical level C1/C2 contralateral to the cancer-related pain.
source: Antero-lateral cordotomy (Bain et al., 2013) was performed at the cervical level C1/C2 contralateral to the cancer-related pain.
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure used in the study.

claim: The cordotomy procedure was performed with sedation and local anesthesia.
source: The procedure was performed with sedation and local anesthesia.
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure used in the study.

claim: Positioning in the spinothalamic tract was verified by eliciting cold, heat or other painful sensations, encompassing the region of cancer-related pain, using 50 Hz electrical stimulation through the cordotomy electrode.
source: Positioning in the spinothalamic tract was verified by eliciting cold, heat or other painful sensations, encompassing the region of cancer-related pain, using 50 Hz electrical stimulation through the cordotomy electrode.
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure used in the study.

claim: Motor twitch threshold using 10 Hz stimulation was performed to assess proximity to the corticospinal tract.
source: Motor twitch threshold using 10 Hz stimulation was also performed to assess proximity to the corticospinal tract.
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure used in the study.

claim: Lesioning of the spinothalamic tract was confirmed in the operating theatre by demonstrating a contralateral loss of temperature sensation on clinical examination.
source: Lesioning of the spinothalamic tract was confirmed in the operating theatre by demonstrating a contralateral loss of temperature sensation on clinical examination.
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure and verification used in the study.

claim: All patients underwent pre-procedure testing, either on the morning of or day before cordotomy.
source: All patients underwent pre-procedure testing, either on the morning of or day before cordotomy.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Post-cordotomy testing was undertaken at least four hours following the procedure to allow for recovery from operative sedation.
source: Post-cordotomy testing was undertaken at least four hours following the procedure to allow for recovery from operative sedation.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: All post-cordotomy assessments were performed within 72 hr of the procedure, when spinothalamic deficits are likely to be maximal.
source: All post-cordotomy assessments were performed within 72 hr of the procedure, when spinothalamic deficits are likely to be maximal.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and rationale.

claim: Pre-procedure and post-procedure testing lasted approximately 90 min.
source: Pre-procedure and post-procedure testing lasted approximately 90 min.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: All assessments were performed on the dorsal aspect of both the right and left forearm.
source: All assessments were performed on the dorsal aspect of both the right and left forearm.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods.

claim: The order of testing with respect to right and left was randomized.
source: The order of testing with respect to right and left was randomized.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Assessment of gentle dynamic touch was made using a 70 mm goat's hair artist brush.
source: Assessment of gentle dynamic touch was made using a 70 mm goat's hair artist brush.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods.

claim: Patients were prevented from seeing the tested extremity throughout the experiment.
source: Patients were prevented from seeing the tested extremity throughout the experiment.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods.

claim: Stimuli were delivered manually in a proximal to distal direction over a 10 cm distance marked on the forearm at velocities of 0.3, 3 and 30 cm s−1.
source: Stimuli were delivered manually in a proximal to distal direction over a 10 cm distance marked on the forearm at velocities of 0.3, 3 and 30 cm s−1, chosen to reflect C-tactile optimal (3 cm s−1) and sub-optimal (0.3 and 30 cm s−1) stimuli.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods.

claim: Six stimuli at each velocity were given on each side in a computer-generated pseudorandom order.
source: Six stimuli at each velocity were given on each side in a computer-generated pseudorandom order.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods.

claim: An inter-stimulus interval of at least 10 s was allowed to prevent fatigue in C-tactile firing.
source: An inter-stimulus interval of at least 10 s was allowed to prevent fatigue in C-tactile firing.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods and rationale.

claim: After each stroke patients rated both the pleasantness and intensity of the stimulation using a 20 cm paper visual analogue scale.
source: After each stroke patients rated both the pleasantness and intensity of the stimulation using a 20 cm paper visual analogue scale.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods.

claim: Cowhage spicules contain the pruritogen mucunain.
source: Cowhage spicules contain the pruritogen mucunain (Reddy et al., 2008; Davidson and Giesler, 2010) and on skin contact induce a histamine independent itch via activation of proteinase-activated receptors-2 and −4 (Reddy et al., 2008; Davidson and Giesler, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Reddy et al., 2008 and Davidson and Giesler, 2010.

claim: Cowhage on skin contact induces a histamine independent itch via activation of proteinase-activated receptors-2 and −4.
source: Cowhage spicules contain the pruritogen mucunain (Reddy et al., 2008; Davidson and Giesler, 2010) and on skin contact induce a histamine independent itch via activation of proteinase-activated receptors-2 and −4 (Reddy et al., 2008; Davidson and Giesler, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Reddy et al., 2008 and Davidson and Giesler, 2010.

claim: Recordings in primates have shown that cutaneous application of cowhage activates ascending spinothalamic projection neurons.
source: Recordings in primates have shown that cutaneous application of cowhage activates ascending spinothalamic projection neurons (Davidson et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Davidson et al., 2012.

claim: Using an F-test power calculator for repeated measures ANOVA, assuming correlation among repeated measures for pleasantness ratings of 0.7, for significance level of 0.05 twenty participants would grant approximately 80% power for an effect size f of 0.25 or 90% power for an effect size f of 0.4.
source: Using an F-test power calculator for repeated measures ANOVA, assuming correlation among repeated measures for pleasantness ratings (primary outcome) of 0.7, for significance level of 0.05 twenty participants would grant approximately 80% power for an effect size f of 0.25 or 90% power for an effect size f of 0.4.
evidence: This describes the sample size calculation for the study.

claim: Previous studies comparing individuals with Hereditary Sensory and Autonomic Neuropathy type V to healthy controls have detected highly significant differences with ten participants per group.
source: Previous studies comparing individuals with Hereditary Sensory and Autonomic Neuropathy type V (a mix of heterozygous and homozygous carriers) to healthy controls have detected highly significant differences with ten participants per group (Morrison et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Morrison et al., 2011.
